notes: "The sage did not show the way down." reads slightly clipped; "The sage did not show him the way down." is more natural.

"He came as a doctor." arrives without any earlier mention of doctors trying to help the princess; adding "Many doctors came, but she did not get better." after "the princess acted mad" would make the disguise clearer.

"acted mad" and "held him close" are the only mildly hard phrases; "acted mad" could become "said strange things and acted like a mad woman" if a simpler wording is wanted. Not enough to block understanding.
"Three sages came from far countries with presents." -> "faraway countries" or "far lands" is more idiomatic.

"There, a king took the princess to his palace. He put the sage in a dark room." gives no reason for jailing the sage; consider "The princess told him, 'This old man stole me.' So the king took her to his palace and put the sage in a dark room."
"a young woman was sleeping on a bed of silk... 'Who are you, and how did you come here?' she asked." skips her waking; consider adding "She woke up and saw him." before the question.
Grammar check: no conditionals or passive found; relative clauses are permitted at B1.

issues.quote: The first brought a brass trumpet that would sound by itself whenever an enemy approached the city gates. Every hour, it spread its tail and cried out. The second brought a golden peacock.
issues.problem: The sentences are in the wrong order: the peacock's behaviour (spreading its tail and crying out every hour) is attached to the trumpet, before the peacock has been introduced. A reader will think the trumpet spreads a tail, which makes no sense and contradicts B1 and C1.
issues.fix: The first brought a brass trumpet that would sound by itself whenever an enemy approached the city gates. The second brought a golden peacock. Every hour, it spread its tail and cried out.

notes: "By bad luck, the sage was walking in that very garden" -> "As bad luck would have it, the sage was walking..." sounds more natural.

"if it truly flew as the sage claimed" is slightly odd because the court has just watched it fly; it works as the king's stalling pretext ("seized gladly on a way to delay"), but "if it truly carried a rider safely, as the sage claimed" would remove the doubt.
"and this time she did not hesitate" implies she hesitated before, which she had no chance to do; "and she did not hesitate" is enough.

summary: A faithful, age-appropriate retelling of the Arabian Nights tale, and A1, A2, B1 and C1 are clean and well levelled. B2 fails on one concrete error: the golden peacock's hourly cry is placed before the peacock appears, so it reads as if the trumpet spreads its tail. Swapping two sentences fixes it.
